p: Ranoji Scindia, also known as Ranoji Sendrak, was born about 1700 into a Maratha family. His father, Jankoji Rao I, was hereditary patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed, a village in the present Satara district of Maharashtra. In earlier centuries his forefathers had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, under the Bahmani Sultanate, and had held jagirs. As a young man he entered the service of Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath. Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar, one of the Peshwa's diplomats, recognised his talents and had him made personal bodyguard to the Peshwa's son, Baji Rao I.

When Baji Rao was appointed Peshwa at the age of twenty by Chhatrapati Shahu, the appointment aroused the jealousy of senior officials at the Maratha court. He therefore promoted talented young men, barely out of their teens, to command his troops, among them Ranoji Scindia, Malhar Rao Holkar, the Pawar brothers, Pilaji Jadhav and Fateh Singh Bhosle. None of them came from families that had held hereditary deshmukhi rights under earlier rulers such as the Deccan Sultanates.

Ranoji was in charge of the Maratha campaign that Baji Rao began in Malwa in 1726, and after it he established his capital at Ujjain in 1731. He appointed Ramchandrababa Sukhtankar as his dewan, or administrator, and Yashaji Rambhaji as commander of his army, and himself spent most of his life on campaign. Some historians credit him with bringing the Kumbh Mela to Ujjain in 1732.

Ranoji died on 3 July 1745. He had five sons: Jayappa Rao, Jyotiba Rao, Dattaji Rao, Tukoji Rao and Mahadji. The four eldest died in battles in northern India between 1750 and 1761. The dynasty went on to dominate central and northern India in the later 18th century through its presence at Delhi, its collection of chauth from neighbouring rulers and a modernised army, and his descendants ruled the princely state of Gwalior under the British.

notes: Short article (about 330 words of substance); the text is near the lower limit.
The article calls him 'the first monarch establishing the Gwalior State as an independent ruler' and also says he served the Peshwas; I kept to the service and the capital at Ujjain.
The article gives the British-period dates for Gwalior as 1810-1947; left out as unexplained.
